name: Latin Dixit Algorizmi
summary: A twelfth-century Latin reworking of al-Khwarizmi's arithmetic, keeping place value, nine numerals and a circle for zero, that carried the method into Europe.
description: Latin reworking of al-Khwarizmi-derived arithmetic, preserving decimal positions, nine numeral signs and a small-circle placeholder; includes operational arithmetic rules.
tier_reason: Retain a distinct Latin transmission/redaction role. Being derived does not make it the Arabic original or justify deletion. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.

places.note: Latin Europe; translation probably in Iberia

date.label: 12th c.
date.basis: Folkerts dates the Latin translation and redaction to the twelfth century; the anchor is a display midpoint. Surviving manuscript copies are later.

events.statement: Latin reworking of al-Khwarizmi-derived arithmetic, preserving decimal positions, nine numeral signs and a small-circle placeholder; includes operational arithmetic rules.
events.place_note: Latin Europe; translation probably in Iberia
events.caveats: Cambridge Ii.6.5 and New York HC 397/726 preserve differing revisions, not the lost first translation. Neither a named translator nor Toledo is asserted as settled.

evidence.locator: Preface PDF p. 9; chapter 4 PDF p. 29; edition §§1.1–1.6 PDF pp. 38–45
evidence.supports: Establishes mediated Latin descent and the actual place-value/empty-place text.

date.label: 13th-century copy
date.basis: Folkerts dates a surviving New York manuscript witness to the thirteenth century.

events.statement: A manuscript copy transmits the Latin Dixit Algorizmi reworking.
events.caveats: The Arabic original is lost and the Latin is mediated; the manuscript date is a scholarly range, not a proven first reception. The surviving witness supports access by its copyist; the copyist’s location and practical execution are not established.

evidence.locator: Chapter 4, PDF p. 29, New York Hispanic Society MS HC397/726 ff. 17r–24v; edition §§1.1–1.6
evidence.supports: Identifies and dates a witness preserving the arithmetical text and numeral/placeholder discussion.

links.statement: The lost Arabic arithmetic was translated into Latin and reworked into the tradition witnessed by Dixit Algorizmi.
links.scope: Ninth-century Baghdad work to twelfth-century Latin translation/redaction, probably Iberia.
links.alternatives: Other contacts and arithmetic texts also transmitted positional calculation.
links.caveats: The precise translator and first Latin wording are unknown; the claim is mediated descent, not a literal unchanged translation.
links.timing: The original work precedes the twelfth-century translation; thirteenth-century witnesses do not redate the translation.
